disclosure: All items are classroom-formative and pre-field-test — not a secure TCAP form; the first cycle of use is what calibrates them.

W.01.stem: Which statement best explains the idea of the divine right of kings?

choices.text: A monarch's authority comes directly from God and cannot be questioned by subjects
A monarch's power is granted and limited by an elected assembly
A monarch must share power equally with the nobility
A monarch is chosen by a popular vote of the people

W.02.stem: What key idea do BOTH the Magna Carta and the English Bill of Rights establish?

choices.text: The monarch's power should be unlimited
The monarch is also bound by law and cannot rule without limits
The monarchy should be abolished entirely
Only the church may limit the king

W.03.stem: John Locke argued that the main purpose of government is to

choices.text: expand the ruler's divine authority
enforce a single official religion
protect people's natural rights to life, liberty, and property
keep power in the hands of the nobility

W.04.stem: One major consequence of the English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution was that

choices.text: England became an absolute monarchy like France
the divine right of kings was strengthened
England abolished Parliament permanently
the English monarch's power became limited by Parliament and law

W.08a.stem: The Declaration of Independence's phrase 'unalienable Rights... Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' most directly reflects the ideas of

choices.text: John Locke
Thomas Hobbes
Louis XIV
Oliver Cromwell

formA.stem: How did Louis XIV use the palace of Versailles to strengthen royal power?

choices.text: By opening it as a meeting place for an elected assembly
By keeping powerful nobles at court and dependent on his favor
By giving the nobility their own regional armies
By turning it into a public university

formA.stem: The Magna Carta (1215) is most significant because it established that

choices.text: Parliament should be abolished
the king's power comes from God alone
even the king is subject to the law
nobles had no legal rights

formA.stem: Which philosopher is correctly matched with his idea?

choices.text: Hobbes — separation of powers
Rousseau — the need for an absolute ruler
Montesquieu — the general will
Locke — natural rights to life, liberty, and property

formA.stem: The English Civil War of the 1640s was fought mainly between supporters of

choices.text: the king and Parliament
France and Spain
two rival churches only
nobles and foreign invaders

formA.stem: Jefferson's phrase 'consent of the governed' is most directly based on the Enlightenment idea that

choices.text: kings rule by divine right
government's authority comes from the people
only nobles may vote
reason cannot guide politics

formB.stem: Peter the Great's policy of westernization was mainly intended to

choices.text: return Russia to older traditions
give the boyars more independent power
modernize Russia using western European technology and institutions
end the monarchy in Russia

formB.stem: Which power did the English Bill of Rights (1689) give to Parliament?

choices.text: the sole right to command the church
ownership of all land
the power to crown foreign kings
control over taxation and free elections

formB.stem: Montesquieu's idea of the separation of powers was designed to

choices.text: divide government so no branch becomes tyrannical
give all power to a single monarch
abolish all government
return power to the church

formB.stem: What made the 1649 execution of Charles I historically significant?

choices.text: It proved the divine right of kings
It showed subjects could hold even a king accountable
It ended all warfare in Europe
It made Cromwell a king

formB.stem: Which Enlightenment thinker most directly influenced the Declaration's ideas about natural rights?

choices.text: Peter the Great
Thomas Hobbes
John Locke
Charles I
